text_blocks.snippet: Plummer's disease, also known as toxic multinodular goiter (MNG), is a condition where the thyroid gland develops multiple nodules that produce excessive thyroid hormone, leading to hyperthyroidism. This overproduction of thyroid hormone can cause a range of symptoms, including weight loss, increased appetite, nervousness, heat intolerance, and more.
snippet_highlighted_words: a condition where the thyroid gland develops multiple nodules that produce excessive thyroid hormone, leading to hyperthyroidism

text_blocks.snippet: What it is: Plummer's disease is a specific type of hyperthyroidism characterized by the presence of multiple autonomous (self-governing) nodules in the thyroid gland. These nodules function independently of the body's normal regulatory mechanisms, leading to excess hormone production.

list.title: Hyperthyroidism:
list.snippet: The excess thyroid hormone can cause a variety of symptoms, including:
Weight loss
Increased appetite
Heat intolerance
Increased sweating
Nervousness and restlessness
Fatigue
Muscle cramps
Irregular menstrual periods (in women)
Frequent bowel movements

list.title: Goiter:
list.snippet: The enlarged thyroid gland (goiter) may be visible or palpable, and in some cases, can cause difficulty breathing or swallowing.
The exact cause of Plummer's disease is not fully understood, but it is thought to be related to genetic factors and long-term iodine deficiency, according to the National Institutes of Health (NIH).
Iodine deficiency can lead to thyroid gland hyperplasia (enlargement) and the development of nodules.
While iodine deficiency is a factor, it's not the sole cause, and other factors like age, gender, and genetics also play a role.

Diagnosis typically involves a physical examination to assess the thyroid gland, blood tests to measure thyroid hormone levels, and nuclear medicine scans (like radioactive iodine uptake) to identify hyperfunctioning nodules.
An ultrasound of the thyroid may also be used to visualize the nodules and assess their characteristics.
Treatment options include radioactive iodine ablation (RIA), which destroys the overactive thyroid tissue.
Antithyroid drugs (like propylthiouracil or methimazole) can be used to manage hyperthyroidism, but they don't address the underlying cause.
Surgery to remove the thyroid gland may be considered in some cases, especially if the goiter is large and causing compression symptoms.
Beta-blockers can be used to manage symptoms like rapid heart rate and tremors.
